CINCINNATI – U.S. Attorney Dominick S. Gerace II announced today results of the Southern District of Ohio’s continuing work to reduce violent crime, firearms offenses and fraud in fiscal year 2026.

Fiscal year 2026 includes Oct. 1, 2025, through Sept. 30, 2026.

Violent and Gun Crime

“I am extremely proud of what my Office has accomplished since I became U.S. Attorney just over a year ago,” said U.S. Attorney Gerace. “My tenure began amid a significant uptick in violent and gun crimes, particularly in downtown Cincinnati, and I promised the public that we would aggressively pursue federal charges against those offenders. The statistics show that we have done just that. I asked my prosecutors to target repeat violent offenders and to focus on the safety of the streets in our communities and they continue to answer the bell.”

As indicated below, in Cincinnati alone, the Office increased prosecutions of firearms offenders by 250% when compared to FY2025. More generally, violent crime prosecutions increased by 148.5% in Cincinnati and by 92.7% districtwide.

The total number of defendants charged with firearms offenses and violent crimes across the District sets a Southern District of Ohio record based on available statistics going back to FY2004. The total number of defendants charged with firearms offenses represents an increase of 93.5% from FY2025.

“None of these cases are possible without strong partnerships with our local, state and federal law enforcement agencies who investigate these crimes. I thank them for joining us in the fight against violence,” said U.S. Attorney Gerace. “I am also grateful to Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson for his continued support and for providing us with a Special Assistant United States Attorney dedicated to federal gun cases.”

Fraud and White-Collar Crime

“The fight against fraud, especially fraud against taxpayer-funded government benefits programs, is a top priority for this Office,” said U.S. Attorney Gerace. “This fiscal year, we brought charges against several individuals who allegedly stole tens of millions of dollars from government programs designed to provide healthcare and food benefits to Americans in need—including a Medicaid fraud scheme involving $30 million and a SNAP fraud scheme involving $29.7 million. As indicated below, the District increased prosecution of white-collar defendants by 46.3% when compared to FY2025, with the largest increases coming from the Dayton and Columbus areas.

We are proud to do our jobs in service to our communities and this great country.”

WASHINGTON — Today, Ambassador Jamieson Greer issued a statement following President Trump notifying Congress and the governments of Rwanda and South Africa of his intent to terminate these countries from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade preference program, as of January 1, 2027.
“The Office of the United States Trade Representative led the annual interagency review of sub-Saharan African countries’ eligibility for the AGOA trade preference program. Based on the review, President Trump found that the governments of Rwanda and South Africa are engaging in practices that are inconsistent with AGOA’s eligibility criteria,” said Ambassador Greer. “These concerning and pervasive practices include, but are not limited to, barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests in the region. The Trump Administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria.”
Background:
In Rwanda, the Trump Administration is deeply concerned by the following issues: trade and investment barriers, rule of law, political pluralism, internationally recognized worker rights, human rights, and threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. In South Africa, the Trump Administration is deeply concerned by barriers to U.S. trade and investment, corruption, and threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

RELEASE: Gottheimer Claws Back $450K from Washington for Englewood’s Dispatch and Emergency Management Center
Funding Will Finish Construction and Equip Departments with Technology for Centralized Emergency Response for Police, Fire, and EMS
Above: Gottheimer announces clawed-back funds in Englewood for Dispatch and Emergency Management Center.
ENGLEWOOD, NJ — Today, Monday, November 2, 2026, Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) announced that he secured $450,000 in federal funding from Washington for the City of Englewood to invest in the completion of its new Dispatch and Emergency Management Center.
Watch full remarks here and facility tour footage here.
“This funding finishes the construction and fits out the technology, so this center can go live. That means the police chief, the fire chief, and our other partners can sit together and run the response to a major storm, fire, or other incident,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5).
The funding will complete construction of the center and fit it out with the technology it needs to go live. Once operational, police, fire, EMS, and city officials will be able to work off the same information in real time during a major storm, fire, or evacuation, with the people making decisions in the same room as the people talking to units on the ground.
Since coming to Congress, Gottheimer has also clawed back $4,099,061 in federal funding for Englewood’s firefighters, including $739,931 through the Assistance to Firefighters Grant (AFG) program and $3,359,129 through the Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response (SAFER) program.
Gottheimer was joined by Bergen County Commissioner Tracy Zur, Englewood Mayor Michael Wildes, Councilwoman Dr. Lisa Wisotsky, Police Chief Thomas Greeley, Deputy Police Chief Matthew De La Rosa, Fire Chief Jeffrey Kaplan, Deputy Fire Chief Kyle Hummel, and City Manager Robert Hoffmann.

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Small Business Administration is reminding eligible businesses, private nonprofit organizations, and residents in Washington of the Nov. 23 deadline to apply for low-interest federal disaster loans to offset physical damage caused by the Chelan Hills wildfire occurring July 4 – 10.
The declaration covers the Washington counties of Chelan, Douglas, Grant, Kittitas, and Okanogan.
Businesses and nonprofits are eligible to apply for physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery, and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
Homeowners and renters are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Applicants may also be eligible for a loan increase of up to 20% of their physical damage, as verified by SBA, for mitigation purposes. Eligible mitigation improvements may include strengthening structures to protect against fire damage, upgrading to wind rated garage doors, and installing a safe room or storm shelter to help protect property and occupants from future damage.
“One distinct advantage of SBA’s disaster loan program is the opportunity to fund upgrades reducing the risk of future damage,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “I encourage businesses and homeowners to work with contractors and mitigation professionals to improve their disaster readiness while taking advantage of our physical damage loans.”
The SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program is available to eligible small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofit organizations — including faith-based organizations — impacted by financial losses directly related to this disaster. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for aquaculture enterprises.
Interest rates can be as low as 4% for businesses, 3.625% for nonprofits, and 2.875% for homeowners and renters with terms up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call SBA’s National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The filing deadline to submit applications for physical damage is Nov. 23. However, after the deadline has passed, there is a 60-day grace period in which SBA will accept applications. The deadline to return economic injury applications is June 22, 2027.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, the SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow, expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.

The Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) will host a research symposium on March 31, 2027, at its headquarters in Washington, D.C. This event will bring together scholars conducting research on demurrage and detention (DnD) practices and policies, as well as industry experts who will share insights regarding the use of DnD to incentivize cargo fluidity and velocity.
The symposium will foster research and discussion that can advance the understanding of DnD practices and their broader economic and operational implications for freight fluidity. The symposium will focus on the following overarching research question: What economic theories or quantifiable frameworks can be developed and used to evaluate the relationships among compensatory costs, DnD charge levels, and the behavioral responses necessary to effectively incentivize cargo movement and freight fluidity?
The FMC is now accepting submission from individuals interested in sharing their papers examining the policies and effects of DnD. The Commission especially encourages the submission of papers that develop and/or evaluate methodologies for setting DnD charges above compensatory costs in order to maintain and demonstrate an effective incentive. Papers may also develop or examine methodologies to assess behavioral responses to DnD charges and how those responses can be deployed to improve cargo velocity and freight fluidity.
Key dates
- Deadline for submissions – February 15, 2027
- Notification to author(s) – March 1, 2027
- Registration opens and agenda announced – March 1, 2027
- Research symposium – March 31, 2027
The research symposium will focus on the following key themes and questions:
Overall incentivizing mechanism:
- Establish a quantifiable economic framework for determining whether, and by how much, DnD charges must differ from actual compensatory costs to effectively incentivize the desired behavioral responses.
- Identify controllable and uncontrollable factors associated with DnD and evaluate how these factors affect charge levels, compensatory costs, and incentive effectiveness.
DnD charges:
- What factors impact the effectiveness of DnD charges as financial incentives?
- Examine how DnD terms and rates are negotiated and determine how contractual relationships, the Incoterms, and/or government holds influence the level and structure of DnD charges.
- Examine decision-making alignment across relevant parties, including whether the party that controls the relevant operational behavior is consistently the party that bears the financial consequences of DnD charges.
Compensatory costs:
- How should compensatory costs associated with DnD be identified, measured, and quantified?
- How can one deploy a quantifiable framework for compensatory costs, including actual costs and opportunity costs, associated with DnD and identify the factors that influence those costs?
Behavioral changes:
- What is the demonstrated relationship between increases in DnD charges and incremental improvements in the desired behavior, and at what point do diminishing returns occur?
- Examine how behavioral responses to DnD incentives translate into improvements in cargo velocity and overall freight fluidity.
If you are interested in submitting a paper, please send an executive summary, extended abstract, or completed paper by February 15, 2027, to Grace Wang at WWang@fmc.gov. You will receive an email confirming receipt of your submission. Preference to participate in the symposium will be given to completed papers.
Accepted participants should expect to receive notification by March 1, 2027. For those interested in attending the conference as audience members, registration will open March 1, 2027. This symposium will be held at FMC Headquarters: 800 North Capitol Street, N.W. Washington, D.C., 20573. For more information or questions, please contact Grace Wang at WWang@fmc.gov and Melina Reilly at MReilly@fmc.gov.
title: FMC will Host a Research Symposium on Demurrage and Detention

NORFOLK, Va. – A Chesapeake woman pled guilty to wire fraud in relation to falsely representing her credentials to provide hair and tattoo removal by laser.

According to court documents, Hayley Nicole Atwood, 33, was licensed by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation as a basic esthetician. Beginning in at least 2017, Atwood consistently falsely purported to be a master esthetician to colleagues and potential customers. Under Virginia law, master estheticians may perform more advanced procedures such as laser hair removal or laser tattoo removal, but only if properly trained and supervised by a licensed physician or physician assistant.

Atwood owned and operated esthetics spas in Chesapeake, Virginia, and Elizabeth City, North Carolina. In March and April of 2021, Atwood purchased two Spectrum Laser devices for her spas. Atwood employed a medical director from December 2019 through July 2021 and a second medical director from July 2021 through November 2022. Neither medical director ever supervised or authorized Atwood or anyone at her business to perform laser tattoo removal. The second director supervised laser hair removal but never evaluated Atwood or her staff or saw her patients. Atwood consistently advertised, offered, and performed laser tattoo and hair removal. Several of Atwood’s clients suffered injury as a result of her laser treatments, including burning and scarring.

Atwood is scheduled to be sentenced on March 5, 2027, and faces up to 20 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia; Marie Maguire, Special Agent in Charge, FDA Office of Criminal Investigations, Metro Washington Field Office; and Col. Jeffrey S. Katz, Superintendent of Virginia State Police, made the announcement after U.S. Magistrate Judge Douglas E. Miller accepted the plea.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Kristen S. Taylor and Rebecca Gantt are prosecuting the case.

Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia or on PACER by searching for Case No. 2:26-cr-83.

Ranking Member Scott Slams ED for Playing Games with Public Service Loan Forgiveness Program
WASHINGTON – Today, House Education and Workforce Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) demanded answers from Department of Education (ED) Secretary Linda McMahon, following concerning reports from borrowers in the Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) program that several qualifying payments were erased from their accounts.
Established in 2007, PSLF offers loan forgiveness to public servants who work for a qualified employer for 10 years and make 120 payments toward their federal student loans. However, borrowers have recently reported that the number of PSLF-qualifying payments, tracked on a counter on the Office for Federal Student Aid’s (FSA’s) website, appeared incorrect. Despite acknowledging the data error, ED failed to provide detailed information on the cause of the error.
“Without additional information from the Department, borrowers cannot know whether changes to the PSLF qualifying payment count were the result of an error that will be fixed; if it is a decision that can be appealed; or if the statement reflects an unappealable decision made by this Administration. Without any additional information, borrowers are left in the dark as to why they must remain in repayment longer than the law requires. This is particularly concerning if a borrower believes they have met all the statutory and regulatory requirements to have their debt forgiven through the PSLF,” wrote Ranking Member Scott.
In his letter, Ranking Member Scott also emphasized that the qualifying payment-count errors come as the Department has not addressed the 88,000-application backlog in the PSLF buyback program and has eliminated affordable repayment plans, creating financial uncertainty and distress for student loan borrowers.
On Friday, October 30, 2026, the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), with support from Protect Borrowers, sued the Trump Administration, alleging it unlawfully blocked student loan forgiveness for tens of thousands of borrowers who qualify. The lawsuit, Weingarten v. McMahon, alleges ED Secretary McMahon mismanaged PSLF by incorrectly counting borrowers’ payment timelines and not awarding people credit for time served.

The Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) announced today a conditional loan commitment of up to $450 million to Neros, Inc., a U.S.-based developer and manufacturer of dual-use small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS).
This investment is intended to support Neros' domestic manufacturing expansion and reduce reliance on foreign-made components.
OSC's conditional loan commitment to Neros directly advances President Donald J. Trump's Executive Order 14307, Unleashing American Drone Dominance. OSC financing alongside additional private capital will support Neros' planned expansion of vertically integrated domestic manufacturing capacity to produce dual-use sUAS platforms, ground control systems, and critical components like motors, radios, flight electronics, sensors, and batteries.
"Neros has already demonstrated an ability to design, manufacture, and deliver exceptional small unmanned aircraft systems," said David A. Lorch, Director of the Office of Strategic Capital and Senior Advisor to Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg. "OSC's investment will turbocharge Neros' ability to manufacture drones and components critical for the production of drone systems."
Neros designs and produces low-cost, high-performance drones. The company's manufacturing facility in Torrance, California will help onshore the production of complete drone systems as well as critical subcomponents including propulsion motors, flight stacks, radios, and thermal sensors. This vertically integrated capacity will support both Neros' internal production and the supply of critical, NDAA-compliant components to other U.S. and allied drone manufacturers.
"Winning the drone industrial-base competition requires the United States to be able to manufacture complete systems at scale and at competitive prices for both military and non-military applications. This starts with bolstering the domestic supply of critical components inside all drone systems," said James R. Shanahan, Senior Managing Director (Investments) at OSC. "Neros' vertically integrated approach would support the creation of significant incremental domestic component capacity for Neros and the broader unmanned-systems ecosystem."
The conditional loan commitment specifies additional steps Neros must complete before financial close, including satisfying various financial, legal, technical, investment, due diligence and other requirements.
"I applaud OSC for helping to strengthen the domestic drone supply chain. Achieving Secretary Hegseth's mandate for American drone dominance requires a secure and resilient industrial base here at home," said Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering.
title: Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital Signs Conditional Loan Commitment of up to $450 Million With Neros, Inc.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today issued final guidance for manufacturers of cellular and gene therapy (CGT) products to implement a comprehensive, science- and risk-based plan for making sure their products meet potency standards. The guidance provides FDA’s recommendations for a Potency Assurance Strategy, which guides manufacturers to test and verify — before a product reaches a patient — that every batch meets a defined standard of potency to do what the product is supposed to do therapeutically.
The Potency Assurance for Cellular and Gene Therapy Products final guidance replaces FDA's 2011 potency testing guidance for CGT products and applies to treatments for serious and often life-threatening conditions. By law, manufacturers are expected to verify that their products work as intended, from the time of approval through post-approval monitoring. This final guidance provides FDA’s current thinking and recommendations on how manufacturers can meet that requirement.
"Patients who receive cellular and gene therapies are often battling serious or life-threatening conditions, such as cancers and rare diseases, and they deserve the assurance that the product administered to them will perform as intended," said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research. "This guidance reflects the FDA's commitment to ensuring America remains the best place in the world to innovate — and that innovation is matched by the highest standards of product quality and patient safety."
The guidance provides flexible, risk-based recommendations for manufacturers on how to integrate potency considerations at every stage of development and commercialization — from early-phase investigational new drug (IND) submissions through biologics license application (BLA) approval and continued post-market verification. Key topics include controls for variability in raw materials, testing during manufacturing, and lab tests that confirm each batch is biologically active in a way that matches its intended therapeutic effect. The guidance also addresses specialized considerations for products with short shelf lives, viral vector gene therapies, and patient-specific therapies.
By giving manufacturers a clear, predictable roadmap, this guidance supports faster access to safe and effective therapies for patients who often have no other treatment options — many of whom receive products made individually for a single person. In doing so, it advances the FDA's public health pillars: protecting patients through rigorous quality standards, promoting innovation by providing regulatory clarity, and reinforcing the integrity of the supply chain for some of the most complex medical products in existence.
The FDA will host a webinar on December 10, 2026, to help stakeholders understand and implement the guidance.
The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.
###
title: November 2, 2026 - FDA Provides Clarity to Support Cell and Gene Therapy Development and Quality

WASHINGTON — Today, the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) announced that it closed Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 with $100 billion in capital and related assistance delivered through its flagship programs. Despite a 43-day federal shutdown that halted SBA lending for nearly two months of the fiscal year, the agency guaranteed 62,205 7(a) and 504 loans totaling $39.5 billion - the third-highest lending volume in agency history, building on the agency’s record-setting year in FY 2025. The SBA’s Small Business Investment Company (SBIC) program closed the year with a record $60 billion in combined private capital and SBA leverage. In addition, the SBA disbursed $192 million in disaster loans to help communities recover and obligated $419 million to support counseling, training, and contracting services for America’s entrepreneurs.
“President Trump’s America First agenda is driving historic growth within the small business economy, including record new business formations in 2026. In turn, small businesses are seeking more capital to hire workers, expand facilities, and supercharge growth,” said SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler. “Despite a federal shutdown that halted SBA lending for nearly two months, the agency delivered its third-highest loan volume on record and closed the year with a record SBIC investment portfolio. And we did that while delivering wins for taxpayers by fighting fraud and restoring prudent lending standards, reversing the Biden Administration’s disregard for statutory requirements of the programs we steward, and their decision to ignore criminal activity in SBA programs. In contrast, the Trump Administration’s Working Family Tax Cuts, deregulation, and fair trade policies reward hard work and investment, instead of punishing those who build Main Street businesses. Through $100 billion in lending, investment capital, disaster relief, and entrepreneurial support, the SBA is delivering for America’s job creators, manufacturers, rural communities, and disaster survivors - helping them grow, rebuild, and strengthen communities nationwide.”
The SBA repeatedly warned that a federal shutdown would sharply constrain access to capital and federal contracting for America’s small businesses. Because the 2025 shutdown froze the 7(a) and 504 programs, SBA could not guarantee an estimated $170 million in loans each business day, totaling roughly $5 billion in financing that otherwise could have been approved during FY26.
Even with that disruption, strong underlying growth in the small business economy continued to drive historic demand for SBA programs and capital. Driven by the Working Families Tax Cuts, fair trade, and deregulation, small businesses across America have started and expanded at record rates throughout 2026. New business formations have exceeded 500,000 in nearly every month this year, while indicators such as the PMI Manufacturing Index show ten straight months of sustained expansion in key sectors.
That growth has translated into historic demand for SBA-backed capital. In FY26, the 7(a) program approved 56,130 loans totaling $32.4 billion, while the 504 program approved 6,075 loans totaling $7.1 billion – a combined 1,350 small business loans each week. The SBA supported over 9,700 startups through the 7(a) and 504 programs, totaling $6.5 billion in financing.
This financing reached the sectors and communities central to the Administration’s economic strength. Lending was strongest in accommodation, retail trade, health care, construction, and manufacturing. Construction and manufacturing businesses received a combined $7 billion through 11,790 7(a) and 504 loans. The SBA also guaranteed 10,314 7(a) and 504 loans totaling $6.5 billion to rural small businesses, expanding access to capital in communities that are essential to America’s domestic production.
Building on that demand, the SBA introduced specialized lending tools to direct capital toward domestic manufacturing, supply-chain resilience, food security, and energy investment. In FY26, the agency approved 149 loans totaling nearly $300 million through its 90% Made in America Guarantee. The new 90% Grocery Guarantee program approved 79 loans totaling $145 million, while the new Manufacturers’ Access to Revolving Credit (MARC) program approved 59 loans totaling $54 million.
As demand for SBA-backed financing grew, so did demand for long-term private investment through the SBIC program. The program closed FY26 with a record $60 billion portfolio in combined private capital and SBA leverage, reflecting continued investor confidence in American entrepreneurs and high-growth small businesses. As part of this record year, the SBA approved 46 new SBIC licenses, cultivating a cohort that is expected to support more than $12 billion in total investment. The agency also approved 35 “Green Light” letters representing conditional pre-approval for SBIC licenses expected to generate another $8 billion in aggregate investment.
The SBA’s FY26 support also extended to communities rebuilding after disaster. The agency approved 5,879 disaster loans totaling $272 million and disbursed 5,371 loans totaling $192 million. Its largest disaster responses supported survivors of Super Typhoon Sinlaku in the Northern Mariana Islands, as well as communities affected by severe winter storms in Mississippi and Tennessee.
To complement capital access and disaster recovery, the SBA obligated $419 million in Entrepreneurial Development Program payments to support its nationwide resource partner network. These investments provide counseling, training, and technical assistance that help entrepreneurs access capital, navigate federal programs, start and grow businesses, and build durable local economies.
# # #

The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of entrepreneurship. Oregon Delegation Celebrates Federal Support for Oregon’s Hazelnut, Seafood Industries
Washington, D.C. – Today, Oregon’s U.S. Senator Jeff Merkley led Oregon Congressional Delegation members—including Senator Ron Wyden and U.S. Representatives Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Val Hoyle (OR-04), Andrea Salinas (OR-06), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), and Janelle Bynum (OR-05)—to announce that after pressure from the delegation, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) will purchase hazelnuts and Pacific Whiting fillets under the agency’s Section 32 purchase program. These purchases will benefit communities and rural economies across Oregon by supporting domestic production and distribution of these agricultural goods during periods of significant market disruption and economic uncertainty.
“Our fisheries and farms deliver incredible products all around the world and are the lifeblood of our communities,” said Merkley, who led the Oregon delegation in pressing USDA to include hazelnuts and whiting in its latest food purchase. “This announcement ensures Oregon’s harvesters, processors, and producers will receive critical financial assistance needed to continue operating and providing services here in Oregon and beyond. I am elated the USDA has decided to make these purchases—this is a win for communities across our state.”
“Iconic state industries like agriculture and fishing count on the U.S. Department of Agriculture to do its job and support Oregonians working hard to keep producing their world-class goods,” said Wyden. “I’m glad the full-court press from the delegation has unlocked this win for Oregonians fishing Pacific whiting and growing hazelnuts.”
“Oregonians know that hazelnuts and seafood are some of the state’s most popular and delicious products,” said Bonamici. “Our growers and producers work tirelessly and bolster the local economy. I’m glad the USDA is making this investment.”
“These investments from the USDA will support the people who harvest, process and bring Pacific Whiting fish and hazelnuts to market,” said Hoyle. “By putting Oregon fishermen and farmers first, we’re boosting our coastal and rural economies."
“Oregon’s specialty crop growers are the backbone of our economy, but too many are struggling with rising costs and uncertain markets,” said Salinas. “In the Willamette Valley, generations of farmers have depended on the hazelnut industry for their livelihoods. That’s why I joined my colleagues in pushing USDA to purchase Oregon hazelnuts and Pacific whiting. These purchases will provide much-needed support for our growers and fishing communities while putting more Oregon-grown and Oregon-caught food onto kitchen tables. I’m proud we secured this win for Oregon producers, and I’ll keep fighting to make sure our specialty crop farmers have the markets and resources they need to succeed.”
"Oregon’s farmers and fishermen work hard to feed our communities, and they deserve a federal government that stands behind them,” said Dexter. “Our delegation pushed USDA to act, and these $34 million in purchases will support Oregon’s hazelnut growers and fishermen during a difficult economic stretch. This investment will help sustain local jobs, strengthen rural and coastal economies, and get nutritious food to families who need it.”
“Our farmers are putting in the work every day to keep Oregon families fed,” said Bynum. “And they’re not just helping put food on the table, they’re keeping money with our families, creating good jobs close to home, and giving people what they need to put down roots here in Oregon. Money back in our state and with our farmers is a win-win.”
Previously, Merkley and the Oregon delegation pressed the USDA to include Pacific whiting and Oregon hazelnuts, which account for 99 percent of hazelnuts produced in the United States, in this year’s Section 32 purchases. Following their efforts, the USDA announced it was purchasing $22 million in hazelnuts and $12 million in Pacific whiting.

Congressman Davis Announces $2.6 Million VA Award for Eastern Carolina State Veterans Cemetery Expansion
WASHINGTON, DC – Congressman Don Davis (NC-01) announced that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs has awarded $2,613,394 to support the expansion of the Eastern Carolina State Veterans Cemetery in Goldsboro.
“Such a historic investment in the Veterans Cemetery Grants Program will help to expand the Eastern Carolina State Veterans Cemetery, allowing more veterans to be laid to rest closer to home,” said Congressman Don Davis.
As a former U.S. Air Force mortuary officer, Congressman Davis remains committed to the support of our veterans, our military families, and the resources and programs available to them. “Our veterans should be able to receive the final honor they so rightfully deserve. They stood for America. We owe them and their families the honor, respect, and dignity they have earned,” Davis added.
The Eastern Carolina State Veterans Cemetery is one of 21 cemeteries across the country that will receive VA cemetery grants in Fiscal Year 2026. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs will also reimburse the cost of pre-placed crypts and their delivery to the cemetery up to $2,878.
The Veterans Cemetery Grants Program is used by states, territories, and Native American tribes to establish, expand, improve, and maintain veterans cemeteries across the country. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs awarded a record $106.5 million in grants through the program in Fiscal Year 2026.
Congressman Don Davis is a 1994 U.S. Air Force Academy graduate and a U.S. Air Force veteran. He serves as the vice ranking member of the U.S. House Armed Services Committee, where he serves on the Readiness and Tactical Air and Land Forces subcommittees.

PICATINNY ARSENAL, N.J. - With decades of fuze experience and knowhow at risk of disappearing as engineers begin to transition out, the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Armaments Center has stepped up to the task of readying the workforce.
Between Monday, Oct. 19 and Friday, Oct. 23, the Armaments Center hosted a course related to munition fuzes for 30 business professionals from small and big business alike. Taught by Senior Fuze Subject Matter Expert Tom Emanski, Acting Army Fuze Management Office Chief Sandy Picinic, Army Fuze Safety Review Board Executive Secretary Briar Ostar-Exel and Armaments Center Fuze Division Engineer Lam Vo, the course provided an open forum for engineers to examine the fundamentals of fuze design, safety philosophies, operational environments and emerging threats, while engaging directly with the experts who help shape military safety standards and evaluations. Fuzes, being the component in a munition that decides when and under what conditions the warhead should function, are a critical component in munitions directly responsible for providing both safety to the warfighter and down range lethality.
According to Emanski, the course was conceived after industrial partners repeatedly signaled how few options there were to learn about fuzing in academia. The field is very rarely taught in traditional academic programs, so many professionals must learn the fundamentals on the job, and while the Armaments Center’s Armament Graduate School (AGS) does have a fuze elective, it is only open to students at the school, making it difficult to preserve knowledge as prior subject matter experts in industry begin to retire. Built from the elective, the course provided training to help both new hires and established professionals develop a shared foundation on fuzes and pass their knowledge forward.
The National Armaments Consortium helped advertise, process applications and coordinate logistics, and Emanski, Picinic and Vo signed on as instructors as they already supported a related elective at AGS. Though the course was planned for some time, it only took about nine weeks to screen applicants and select attendees, Emanski said. The course was capped to 30 students to preserve interactive two-way discussion and deep learning, as any larger would approach a lecture.
“It’s to help as a starting point to understand this very unique item called ‘fuze’, which plays a critical role in our munitions,” noted Picinic.
During the course, attendees received a basic overview of fuzes, delved into the fundamentals of fuze safety design architectures and environments, discussed hand-placed ordnance, target detection, among other topics. The syllabus also addressed the ever-changing landscape of unmanned systems, in which fuzes are a quintessential component, and explained both electronic and mechanical aspects.
“Fuzes are on just about every munition out there. It’s challenging to teach a course when there’s so many use cases,” said Emanski. “Each fuze for every commodity item is different, so we’re teaching a course where there are many different examples, use cases and CONOPs (concepts of operation).”
The students themselves came from both small and large businesses; some had a decade of experience with fuzes, while others had never touched one before. This spectrum of experience, alongside the wide variety in business backgrounds, led to meaningful engagement throughout the week.
“My group designs and builds seekers and tracking missile interceptors. We're expanding our capabilities, and this was an area identified as a key gap where we wanted to deepen our expertise,” said Boeing Integrated Air and Missile Defense engineer Erik Stein.
Several students noted not only the broad omnibus, but how different the course was from what they expected. Falcata AI Engineer Adam Tuck showed surprise at spending a full day talking about interrupted fuzes, which use purely mechanical components to keep the fuze from setting a munition off too early, and non-interrupted fuzes, which use electronics. Wild West Systems Chief Engineer of Munitions and Energetics John Granier called the discussion about balancing cost and safety “fascinating,” while TETAC Incorporated Chief Executive Officer Mark Benson noted the section on fuze safety boards and how it humanized a force usually unseen.
Participants praised the course universally for offering information otherwise not available to industry and expressed hope that a similar course would be offered again in the future.
“I think a lot of the reason why this is so niche is that there’s no awareness of this at the collegiate level. It’d be cool, now that we’re opening this up to industry, if that eventually bleeds down to universities and maybe gets more people interested earlier on rather than as we go through our careers. I didn’t know what a fuze was when I started,” said Day and Zimmermann Munitions Director of Business Development Christopher Stemple.
According to Emanski, there have already been inquiries from industry members about when the Armaments Center can offer the course again in the future. Seeing the success of the course, the Armaments Center has already started working with NAC representatives and industry to expand the course offering in 2027.
title: Armaments Center hosts first industry fuzing course to preserve critical expertise

The Department of the Air Force’s Spark Tank program concludes its final year with the Top 5 ideas selected out of 350 total submissions. These ideas endured strict subject matter evaluation from 1,394 members casting nearly 26,000 votes, evaluation from command leadership, and final determination by a panel of innovation leaders.
Out of 350 total submissions from across the Air and Space Forces, the Spark Tank 2026 Top 5 are:
Automated Master Storage Plan (Air Combat Command) – Leverages artificial intelligence to plan warehouse layouts for munitions, enabling weeks of planning to be executed in minutes.
M-UAS-D, MANET-enabled UAS Detector (Air Combat Command) – Low-cost for large scale deployment, a counter sUAS to detect drones, share real-time range data to users and response teams.
Project CAPYBARA (Air Mobility Command) – A set of tutorials and parts lists provided to any organization to build custom rovers for any capability needed in the field, replacing costly TDYs and certification programs.
Secure STIG Checker (Air Force Special Operations Command) – Replaces Enterprise Network manual compliance checks with a tool capable of analyzing millions of lines of code in under 500 seconds.
Tac-Hub: Agile Communications for the Modern Mission (Air Force Global Strike Command) – Modular command and control suite to enable rapid deployment; designed for military and emergency response teams.
Spark Tank is the Department of the Air Force's premier campaign where Guardians and Airmen present their innovative solutions to top leaders and industry experts, seeking sponsorship to bring their concepts to life.
The Top 5 teams will now accelerate prototypes and forge strategic partnerships with the help of AFWERX Refinery and DAF Enterprise Innovation support.
A panel of judges also reviewed the following semi-finalist submissions, which will be migrated for support and progression:
Aerial Minefield (Air Combat Command) – Low cost solution to create dense clouds of aerial obstacles to defend against and disable low-cost adversarial drones.
Agile Cyber Training Environment: Portable Cyber Ops Center (Air Combat Command) – Portable, battery-powered, network-independent center globally deployable by a single person in less than a minute for agile cyber operations.
Contingency Remote Optical Charging Spacecraft (Space Systems Group) – Charges dead spacecraft with ground lasers to prevent abandoned spacecraft and lost satellites due to loss of power.
Energy Resilience Command Platform (Air Force Reserve Command) – Dashboard unifying all base energy, power, water, heating, and mission critical data into a real time “Base Resilience Percentage”, indicating operational sustainment during disruptions.
Flight Room 3D Models (Air Education and Training Command) – Standardizes and institutionalizes 3D printed models of pilot curriculum items.
Project HOPLITE (Air Force Special Operations Command) – Integrates key components from Land Phalanx Weapon System, tactical truck, or FMTV load handling system to create a flexible and rapidly deployable air defense solution, transportable by C-130.
(ReSearch) an Advanced Search Engine for EPubs (Air Force Material Command) – Integrates Advana’s advanced search engine, natural language processing, and data analytics into the EPubs platform to allow Airmen to find exactly what they are looking for.
SpartReg 36-2903 Pictures of Dress Right vs. Wrong (Pacific Air Forces) – Digital interactive guide with side-by-side “correct vs. incorrect” examples, hyperlinks, and visual decision trees for dress and appearance standards.
Streamline 1205 Narrative Sync (Pacific Air Forces) – Standardize Air Force writing style by switching from character count format that matches EPB/ORB narrative standards.
The Sheppard Blueprint: A Proven Model for CONUS MTF Pharmacy Recapture (Air Education and Training Command) – Low-cost and highly replicable, a text message outreach and 24/7 prescription lockers to prevent lost cost in on-base pharmacies.
Vehicle Diagnostic System (Air National Guard) – Consolidates 5 tools and 7 software licenses into 1 tool for vehicle diagnostics.
title: DAF announces Spark Tank 2026 Top 5

MONROE – On October 21, 2026, United States Chief District Judge Terry A. Doughty sentenced Justavious K. “Tae Tae” Williams , 25, of Bastrop, to 336 months in federal prison for Conspiracy to Possess a Controlled Substance with Intent to Distribute and for Possessing a Firearm in Furtherance of a Drug Trafficking Crime, followed by five years of supervised release. Williams previously pled guilty to the charges on July 10, 2026.

According to court documents, between May 16, 2025, and October 9, 2025, Williams participated in a methamphetamine trafficking organization. Investigators executed a wiretap on one of Williams’ co-conspirator’s phones and intercepted calls and messages in which Williams discussed acquiring and distributing large quantities of methamphetamine. On October 1, 2025, communications revealed that Williams’ co-conspirators were arranging the pickup of a large shipment of methamphetamine from Texas. Williams then traveled to Garland, Texas, where agents observed him and a co-conspirator load a bright orange suitcase into a vehicle. After the vehicle returned to Louisiana, Louisiana State Police (LSP) later attempted a traffic stop. Williams fled the stop, leading troopers on a brief pursuit before Williams and the co-conspirator were caught and arrested. A search of the vehicle revealed approximately 25 kilograms of methamphetamine in the suitcase. Roughly a week later, Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agents executed a search warrant at a local address where Williams was found with the same co-conspirator as in the car stop. Inside the residence, agents recovered seven firearms along with various quantities of ecstasy pills, methamphetamine, marijuana, and other controlled substances. A cook lab trailer located behind the residence contained 20,000 methamphetamine pills and more than three kilograms of additional powder methamphetamine.

U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement.

The case was investigated by DEA, LSP, and Monroe Metro Narcotics. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney J. Aaron Crawford with assistance from Legal Assistant Amanda Morgan.

You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer, under Case Number 3:25 cr 299.

FORT WAINWRIGHT, Alaska — From hand-sewn prototypes to custom-built web platforms, Soldiers of the 11th Airborne Division demonstrated the power of grassroots innovation during Angel Ascent, held Oct. 28 at the division theater.
Col. Matthew Adamczyk, Deputy Commanding Officer for Operations, 11th Airborne Division, praised the competitors’ efforts.
“Soldiers across the 11th Airborne Division continue to demonstrate that many of the best ideas come from the bottom up. Events like Angel Ascent prove the ability of our troops to solve problems, our job is to help provide the right resources. When our Soldiers and leaders are empowered, there's no limit to what we can achieve in the Arctic and beyond.” said Col. Adamczyk.
Spc. Leighton Keilen, 1st Battalion, 24th Infantry Regiment, 1st Infantry Brigade Combat Team, 11th Airborne Division, earned first place for his Skydio Drone Relay and modular payload delivery system that significantly extends tactical drone range and utility in Alaska’s rugged, mountainous terrain. Col. Matthew Adamczyk presented Keilen with a Meritorious Service Medal. All other competitors received Army Commendation Medals, and every participant was awarded a four-day pass in recognition of their efforts.
The competition provided Soldiers of all ranks a direct platform to present practical solutions to senior military leaders, civilian officials and innovation experts. Each innovator received 10 minutes to brief their project followed by five minutes of questions from the judging panel, which evaluated entries on problem identification, solution quality, operational value, resource requirements and presentation.
The event highlighted a key truth: some of the Army’s most effective solutions come from the Soldiers who live with the problems every day. Whether serving in Arctic extremes or supporting complex administrative demands, these warfighters refused to accept “the way it’s always been done.”
The competitors’ backgrounds highlight the wide range of skills, experiences and perspectives that strengthen today’s Army. Pfc. Michael Pereira, a Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems specialist from Miami, Florida, hand-sewed his first prototype of a passive thermal battery vault designed to keep drone batteries viable in sub-zero temperatures using only body heat and radiant barriers. Staff Sgt. Baddeley, a respiratory therapist from Petaluma, California, developed TroopToTask.org after years of watching small-unit leaders struggle with fragmented spreadsheets. His intuitive web platform consolidates personnel data, training records, duty rosters and mission tracking, allowing commanders, first sergeants and leaders at every echelon to focus on leading Soldiers instead of chasing administrative tasks.
Other standout projects included a low-cost battery eliminator for PRC-158 radios in extreme cold, a modular power and heating system for man-hauled Ahkio sleds, 3D-printed explosively formed penetrators for FPV drones, and a unit-fabricated ring mount hatch for FMTVs that protects convoy gunners in Arctic conditions for a fraction of the cost of commercial systems.
By formally recognizing these efforts with awards and command emphasis, the 11th Airborne Division is cultivating a culture where initiative is expected and innovation is accelerated. Events like Angel Ascent serve as a powerful example for the broader Army of how to empower Soldiers at the tactical edge to solve real problems, reduce logistical burdens, and increase lethality in austere environments.
title: Soldiers from across 11th Airborne Division shine at Angel Ascent innovation competition

The National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) today announced the appointment of Amy L. Cocuzza as the new Solicitor. Ms. Cocuzza is now the chief legal advisor and consultant to the entire Board on all questions of law regarding the Board’s general operations and on major questions of law and policy concerning the adjudication of NLRB cases in the Courts of Appeals and the U.S. Supreme Court. She also serves as the Board’s legal representative and liaison to the General Counsel and other offices of the Board.

Ms. Cocuzza brings to the Board more than two decades of experience in labor law, administrative law, and workplace relations. She began her legal career as an Honors Attorney for then-NLRB General Counsel Ronald Meisburg, gaining experience with various GC-side branches including Regional Advice, Appeals, and Appellate and Supreme Court Litigation, as well as the Region 5 Washington Resident Office. She went on to spend nearly a decade with the Division of Advice, rising from staff attorney to supervisory attorney before moving Board-side.

Most recently, Ms. Cocuzza was the Acting Chief of Staff to Board Chairman James R. Murphy. Prior to that, she served as Deputy Solicitor to former Solicitor Fred B. Jacob, who recently became Chief Counsel to Board Member David M. Prouty.

“With her years of experience at the NLRB and in the Solicitor’s Office, Amy will bring legal prowess, institutional wisdom, and diplomatic savvy to her new position as the Board’s Chief Legal Advisor,” said former Solicitor Fred Jacob. “Amy is committed to the NLRB’s mission and the public we serve. The Board is lucky to have her.”

Board Chairman James Murphy notes: “Former Solicitor Fred Jacob set a high standard for excellence in the performance of his duties in that office. We are very fortunate to have someone like Amy Cocuzza as a successor so worthy and qualified to uphold that standard.”

Board Member Dave Prouty remarked: “Amy Cocuzza is the right person at the right time to take on this tremendously important job at the Board. I look forward to relying on her wise counsel as “The Board’s Lawyer” for many years to come.”

Ms. Cocuzza received her B.S. in Human Biology from the University at Albany (SUNY), her Master of Industrial and Labor Relations from Cornell University, and her J.D. from the University of Michigan Law School, where she served as Editor-in-Chief of the University of Michigan Journal of Law Reform. Prior to attending law school, Ms. Cocuzza spent several years organizing with labor unions in New York City, representing healthcare workers with 1199 SEIU and professional musicians with Local 802, American Federation of Musicians. She has also taught labor law at the Antonin Scalia Law School of George Mason University.

Established in 1935, the National Labor Relations Board is an independent federal agency that protects employees from unfair labor practices and protects the right of private sector employees to join together, with or without a union, to improve wages, benefits and working conditions. The NLRB conducts hundreds of workplace elections and investigates thousands of unfair labor practice charges each year.
title: Amy L. Cocuzza Named Solicitor to the National Labor Relations Board

OPM Review Identifies $106.7 Million in Improper Payments in FEHBP
WASHINGTON, DC – The US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has identified approximately 50,000 deceased individuals who remain listed in the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program (FEHBP) by matching Treasury’s August 2026 Death Record Confidence Scoring Tool (DRCST) against OPM’s FEHB enrollment records.
The review identified $96.3 million in improper payments made after date of death, including $70.6 million in government FEHB premium contributions and $25.7 million in retirement payments.
OPM also estimates $10.4 million in carrier costs tied to over 20,000 individuals who remain on carrier rolls even though no government premium is being paid for them. Carriers charge FEHB funds each month for administrative and per-member costs. OPM will examine claims that may have been paid after date of death in the coming weeks.
“Every outdated enrollment record can carry a cost. This review is helping us find those records, identify payments that need action, and reduce unnecessary costs to FEHB,” OPM Associate Director of Healthcare and Insurance Matthew Kiley said.
“We will not allow the taxpayer to shoulder the burden of fraud, waste, or improper payments. These findings are a drop in the bucket of what we expect to find as we double down on our integrity program,” OPM Director Scott Kupor said.
“Here is a simple rule only President Trump and Vice President Vance understand: Dead people should not receive health benefits. Today is another critical step forward in reversing the errors by the previous administration,” Executive Director of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud Scott Bradysaid.
title: OPM Review Identifies $106.7 Million in Improper Payments in FEHBP

WASHINGTON — Seeking to disrupt how the military funds modernization, Marc Andersen, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Financial Management and Comptroller, declared that the service must "move at the speed of capitalism" to outpace global adversaries. Speaking at the Association of the United States Army 2026 Annual Meeting, Oct. 15, 2026, Andersen championed the Strategic Capital Initiative as a permanent institutional shift to align national security priorities with commercial business cases.
Throughout the panel discussion, Andersen reinforced that SCI is not just another pilot program, but a fundamental shift in how the Army approaches public-private collaboration. A primary focus of his remarks was the concept of de-risking investments for public-private partnerships to create certainty for both the warfighter and the investor. Andersen explained that private capital requires financial predictability the same as military requires operational certainty that a capability will work when needed. By leveraging creative, long-term enhanced use leases, the Army can provide the stable environment necessary to attract significant private investment, effectively aligning national security priorities with commercial business cases.
To execute this vision, Andersen stressed that the Army must operate at the "speed of capitalism" rather than relying on rigid, transactional procurement models. He called for a shoulder-to-shoulder collaboration model grounded in open, early communication where both sides can discuss constraints honestly. This cultural shift requires a significant investment of time and energy to build mutual understanding, which Andersen argued is the only way to move fast enough to counter modern strategic adversaries.
Equally important to this mission is the institutional endurance of the initiative itself. Andersen noted that while individual leaders are only in their roles for a brief period, the structures established by the SCI must outlive them to create a permanent, healthier, and more diverse industrial base. To ensure this long-term success, his team is actively working to overcome legacy bureaucracy by carefully distinguishing between actual statutory laws and mere historical norms or policy behaviors that have frozen procurement processes over time.
By aggressively challenging these internal preferences, the Army aims to create a frictionless pathway that avoids the slow, bureaucratic traps of the past. Andersen said “We’re actively hunting policy, to reduce friction, increase velocity and move at the speed of trust to properly resource our Army to fight and win or nation’s wars. As we rebuild our Arsenal of Democracy, we are grounded in deterrence while ensuring our Warfighters never enter a fair fight.”

ADELPHI, Md. — Years of Army scientific research culminated in the successful flight demonstration of a 3D-printed heavy-fuel rotary-engine series-hybrid system, advancing power and propulsion science for future tactical unmanned aircraft systems.
Researchers at the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command, known as DEVCOM, Army Research Laboratory, designed the advanced drone propulsion through its Versatile Tactical Power and Propulsion essential research program.
"The program addresses critical power and propulsion challenges by advancing fundamental science that could enable drones to fly longer and faster, operate at higher altitudes, carry heavier payloads and perform in extreme environments while reducing logistics burdens," said Dr. Chol-Bum “Mike” Kweon, DEVCOM ARL program manager. "For warfighters, the program has transitioned research findings to industry partners for maturation and integration into capabilities that could enable mid-sized drones to operate beyond line of sight, extending the reach of ground commanders and reducing risk to Soldiers."
ARL researchers used advanced computational fluid dynamics modeling and a clean-sheet design approach to address the challenges of efficiently burning heavy fuel in a rotary engine. The work improved fuel atomization and vaporization while minimizing compressed-air and fuel-vapor leaks.
“The use of advanced manufacturing, including 3D metal printing, allowed us to rapidly redesign engine components based on lessons learned through experimentation,” Kweon said. “It enabled us to design an air-cooled engine that reduces propulsion-system size and eliminates the need for liquid coolant.”
Integrated with a novel 400-volt motor-generator system, the engine forms a heavy-fuel rotary-engine series-hybrid system designed to support vertical takeoff and landing operations in contested environments.
To demonstrate the propulsion system in flight, ARL worked with industry partners, including Griffon Aerospace, to develop an aircraft platform around the propulsion system. The novel series hybrid system powers the Group 3 midsized, unmanned aircraft system, Versatile Intelligence Controlled Tactical Operational Reconnaissance and Attack, or VICTOR UAS.
The VICTOR essential research program generated many additional outcomes for the Army, industry and academia, including:
- Collaborative research with more than 30 universities, more than 13 federal laboratories and more than 20 industry partners that resulted in hundreds of scientific journal publications in diverse areas including combustion chemistry, sensing and controls, material design, batteries and hybrid electric technology
- Professionally developed hundreds of scientists and engineers now working in government, industry and academia
- Research advances that address energy and propulsion challenges relevant to tactical-level energy independence
- Technical data packages, design methods and reliability lessons applicable to future propulsion and drone design and integration efforts
- Tens of patents and patent applications
Lessons from the essential research program will inform follow-on ARL research and industry development efforts, including the Persistent Unmanned Aircraft System for Logistics, Strike, Autonomy, and Reconnaissance, or PULSAR, an advanced drone-operation concept that enables multi-mission capabilities through a swarm of VICTOR drones.
The VICTOR UAS and the PULSAR concept will be made available to military partners for further experimentation and development. Industry partners will continue refining VICTOR UAS for other applications.
─────────────────────────
DEVCOM ARL is the Army’s sole fundamental research laboratory serving as the nexus of science between the military, academia and industry. Operating under the U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, ARL executes globally recognized research to accelerate delivery of war-winning, disruptive technologies for tomorrow’s Army.
For information, visit the Army Research Laboratory website.
title: Army research leads to first 3D-printed heavy-fuel engine

Remarks

Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun, Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism Office of the Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism

Buenos Aires, Argentina

November 1, 2026

As Prepared.

Thank you, Ambassador Fabiana Loguzzo, Mr. Marcelo Mindlin, Secretary General Michaela Küchler, Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Latino Coalition for Israel, and the Latin American Jewish Congress for hosting this important convening.

Just minutes from this room, the Jewish diaspora suffered its deadliest terrorist attack since the Holocaust. On July 18, 1994, Iranian-backed Hizballah terrorists bombed the AMIA Jewish community center. They murdered 85 innocent people and wounded more than 300. Thirty-two years later, the victims’ families, the Argentine people, and Jewish communities around the world are still seeking justice.

It means something that we gather here, under Argentina’s historic IHRA presidency, to discuss the role of the state in combating antisemitism. Once a refuge for Nazi war criminals and a bastion of antisemitic terror, Argentina has shown us what happens when a government decides to act. Under my good friend President Milei, and together with Foreign Minister Quirno, Argentina has designated Hamas and the IRGC as terrorist organizations; pursued a trial in absentia against the perpetrators of the AMIA terrorist attack; and hosted the launch of the U.S.-led Global Guidelines for Countering Antisemitism.

Argentina stands together with the United States in leading boldly and unapologetically to protect Jewish communities worldwide. Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio, the United States is reversing four years of bureaucratic handwringing and shameful inaction by acting decisively to protect Jewish communities. We have confronted antisemitism on university campuses; reinvigorated hate crime prosecutions; implemented rigorous visa vetting to prevent foreign nationals from fomenting hatred; withdrawn from antisemitic international organizations and held UNRWA accountable; and unlike the previous administration, we have made clear that the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism, inclusive of its examples, is the only definition this administration supports.

My office was proud to spearhead an interagency effort to arrest Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, a radical Islamist who claimed responsibility for multiple attacks and attempted plots throughout Europe earlier this year and who sought to do the same across the Western Hemisphere. “The role of the state,” as President Trump and Secretary Rubio have shown, is an uncompromising one. Now we are urging our partners to follow suit.

When you fight antisemitism, good news is rare. Under Argentina’s presidency, however, real change is taking root across our hemisphere. We congratulate Paraguay for pursuing IHRA membership and thank the Dominican Republic and Peru for endorsing the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism, inclusive of its examples, as well. From Colombia to Bolivia, Chile to Costa Rica, and Panama to Guatemala, governments across the region are taking a stand and tackling this scourge.

Beyond our hemisphere, Armenia too has expressed its willingness to join IHRA. We are now finding partners in regions where progress once seemed impossible. As antisemitism fuels violence and terror around the world, governments across the Middle East and North Africa are showing what happens when a state decides to act. Saudi Arabia has addressed concerning themes in textbooks and school curricula; Morocco has expanded Holocaust education in schools and opened a Jewish museum; and the United Arab Emirates participated for the first time ever in the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism Forum in Dublin just last month.

Yet while these governments make tremendous strides, too many of our European partners are failing to fulfill their commitments to protect Jewish communities. It is shocking that they keep their seats at the table while many of the governments now leading the way remain outside it. Some are prevented from joining — that is a double standard. Others are new to this fight — that is an opportunity.

Once again, too many of our European partners are failing to lead in the way in the fight against hatred. Too many seem satisfied with the status quo — simply checking a box to say “we did it.” After a year of lethal attacks targeting Jewish communities worldwide, none of us can say that the status quo is working. None of us can say that checking a box is working.

Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio, the United States will not simply check a box. We want to see real, decisive change. That is why the United States urges IHRA and other bodies in the fight against antisemitism to build on Argentina’s historic efforts. Rather than gate keep participation, we need to prioritize expanding the global reach of our coalition. Any government that is serious about countering antisemitism, promoting Holocaust remembrance and education, and standing with Jewish communities should have a seat at the table.

Can any European government tell this body that they are fighting hatred better than the Emiratis? Can any government say that Saudi Arabia improving its curricula is not a historic opportunity to expand our coalition against hatred?

The threat is too urgent to turn away allies in this fight.

Since my first day in office as the United States Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism, I have said that every civilized country should be a member of this body. To every government that is not yet an IHRA member, including the many governments from Latin America here today, we urge you: pursue IHRA membership and endorse the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism, inclusive of its examples. Together with the Global Guidelines for Countering Antisemitism, these steps show that your government is ready to lead in this fight.

The success of IHRA, or any multilateral body, however, will be measured not in its ability to make commitments. To commit to do something is easy. To check a box is even easier. Our success will be measured only in our ability to implement those commitments. That is why we ask everyone here who already has joined IHRA: are you actually living up to what being a part of this global coalition demands?

If your government has endorsed the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism, inclusive of its examples, are you implementing policies that apply “double standards by requiring of [Israel] a behavior not expected or demanded of any other democratic nation”? And if your government is looking to single out Israel, what are you doing to hold the Palestinian Authority accountable for its antisemitic behavior, including promoting Holocaust distortion? What are you doing to ensure it ends pay-for-slay and holds free and fair elections? And what are you doing to ensure Hamas disarms? Whether its rioters burning American and Israeli flags in the streets of France or excessive sanctions regimes in countries like Norway, Israel should not be the scapegoat.

If your government has endorsed the U.S.-led Global Guidelines for Countering Antisemitism, have you adopted a national strategy or action plan and appointed a designated envoy or coordinator with the necessary empowerment and resources to be effective? And as if the issue was not big enough, for how many envoys or coordinators are antisemitism and Holocaust issues just one small part of your other mandates?

And if your government is a participating State of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe and has endorsed the 2004 Berlin and 2014 Basel declarations, are you collecting and reporting disaggregated antisemitic hate crime data? And if you are collecting that data, are you actually using it to craft your policy response?

The role of the state does not end in making commitments, endorsing definitions, or joining a multilateral body like IHRA. That is where it begins. That is where it starts.

Your responsibility as government officials, envoys and coordinators, IHRA delegates, and community leaders is to lead — to remind your government of its own moral obligations. Leadership is not comfortable. Leadership is not easy. But lead we must.

Allow me to share a brief thought about the rules of kashrut. The definition of a kosher fish is outlined clearly by God in the bible: a fish must have fins and scales. But there is another unwritten requirement — not written in the Bible — which many people forget: a fish found floating on top of the water is not kosher. A kosher fish must be alive when it is caught. It must swim against the stream. Against the current. My fellow government officials, envoys and coordinators, IHRA delegates, and community leaders: the time to swim against the current is now.

Now is not the time to conform to the status quo. To resort to exclusionary mindsets that make no sense. Let us lead. Let us work together with any country that stands with us.

When Hitler rose to power in 1933, we did not have strong leaders like President Trump or President Milei who were ready to confront this evil head-on. We know all too well what happens when real leadership gives way to appeasement, abdication, and complicity.

A government is judged by how it keeps law and order — how it ensures that every citizen is safe and secure. I urge everyone here to ask yourselves: is my government doing all that it can to ensure Jews feel safe in my country? Or can we do better?

As President Trump said last year during the Days of Remembrance, “We declare that never again means now.” Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio, the United States affirms that expanding the frontiers of remembrance cannot and must not end at the conclusion of this plenary. It requires a sustained commitment to expanding the breadth of our global coalition and the depth of our action.

I extend my sincerest gratitude and congratulations to our Argentine hosts and wish everyone a productive plenary. Thank you.

Bonamici, Wyden, Merkley Demand Investigation into ICE Tire Slashing Incident
WASHINGTON, DC [11/2/26] – Today Congresswoman Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01) and Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley demanded an investigation into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents for slashing a couple’s tires in Hillsboro.
The couple was observing and recording ICE agents in a supermarket parking lot on October 7, 2026, before multiple masked ICE agents in three vehicles tailed the couple, boxed them in, and repeatedly stabbed and slashed their tires before driving away. A video of the incident can be viewed here.
“ICE agents cannot act with impunity,” the lawmakers wrote. “The First Amendment protects the right to observe, gather information, and record law enforcement officers performing their duties in public. These constitutional protections are necessary for the public to learn about and freely debate the government’s actions, including potential misconduct, and demand accountability when necessary.”
The lawmakers noted that there have been many documented cases of excessive use of force and intimidation tactics against peaceful community members and legal observers by ICE in Oregon and across the country. They called for the Inspector General for the Department of Homeland Security to immediately investigate the Oct. 7 incident in Hillsboro, identify the agents involved, and preserve all evidence, so that those responsible may be disciplined.
“Without videos from bystanders, observers, journalists, and protestors, the public would never know the full scale of federal retaliation against those who seek to document ICE activity,” the lawmakers wrote.
Bonamici, Wyden, Merkley, and Dexter also recently raised concerns about the lack of access to counsel for individuals detained by ICE and what appear to be new protocols for bypassing the Portland ICE facility entirely. That letter can be found here.
The full letter about the Oct. 7 incident can be read here and below:
Dear Inspector General Cuffari:
We write to request an investigation into an alarming incident that occurred on October 7, 2026, in which U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents harassed, intimidated, and retaliated against a couple in Hillsboro, Oregon for engaging in First Amendment activities. The incident occurred when our constituents observed and recorded ICE agents in a supermarket parking lot. Soon thereafter, multiple masked ICE agents in three vehicles recklessly tailed the couple, boxed them in, and dangerously vandalized their vehicle by repeatedly stabbing and puncturing one of their tires before driving away.1
ICE agents cannot act with impunity. The First Amendment protects the right to observe, gather information about, and record law enforcement officers performing their duties in public.2 These constitutional protections are necessary for the public to learn about and freely debate the government’s actions, including potential misconduct, and demand accountability when necessary.
Since President Trump returned to office in January 2025, federal ICE agents across the country have repeatedly failed to respect rights afforded under the Constitution, especially the First Amendment. We have seen many documented cases of excessive use of force and intimidation tactics by ICE in Oregon, including federal agents needlessly deploying tear-gas and other projectiles against peaceful community members as well as driving erratically and verbally threatening legal observers. This pattern of irresponsible and illegal behavior from federal agents is also evident across the country. For example, federal agents in Memphis, Tennessee harassed observers by swerving at them, tailing them, boxing them in, and pulling them over without reasonable suspicion; sitting outside of their homes; and assaulting and arresting them.3 In Los Angeles, federal agents fired crowd control weapons into the heads and other sensitive areas of observers, journalists, and protestors. A judge later granted an injunction against this behavior4 and found that the plaintiffs have plausibly alleged that DHS had a policy of retaliating against people who record the activities of agents.5
Most troubling, federal immigration agents killed Alex Pretti while he was peacefully recording and protesting ICE’s actions.6 Through all of this, the Trump administration has repeatedly covered up officer misconduct and obstructed investigations.7 To this day, there is no evidence that the federal government has meaningfully investigated Mr. Pretti’s killing, with his parents noting that “at every turn, they have ignored us, misled us and shielded Alex’s killers.”8 This reckless behavior and senseless violence endangers everyone across the country and does not advance ICE’s mission of enforcing immigration laws to preserve national security and public safety.
Without videos from bystanders, observers, journalists, and protestors, the public would never know the full scale of federal retaliation against those who seek to document ICE activity.
We hereby demand that your offices immediately undertake an investigation of the October 7, 2026, incident in Hillsboro, Oregon outlined above. Please identify the ICE agents involved and preserve all relevant evidence so the officers can be disciplined and prosecuted as appropriate.
Further, we request that you undertake a comprehensive investigation of the pervasive pattern of ICE agents acting unlawfully and retaliating against individuals exercising their First Amendment rights. We ask that you work with Congress to make lasting changes to ICE training, oversight, and accountability. The rights of our constituents must not be jeopardized any longer.
Sincerely,
###
